title: Linear Transformations and Their Matrices
summary: A matrix multiplies vectors; but a matrix is also a function. The map $\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ rotates, stretches, projects or reflects space, and linear algebra is, at heart, the study of such maps. This chapter defines linear transformations on…

intro.x: A matrix multiplies vectors; but a matrix is also a function. The map $\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ rotates, stretches, projects or reflects space, and linear algebra is, at heart, the study of such maps. This chapter defines linear transformations on arbitrary vector spaces, proves that every one is represented by a matrix once bases are fixed, and shows that composition of maps corresponds to matrix multiplication. That explains why matrix multiplication is defined the way it is.

blocks.x: Let $V,W$ be vector spaces over $\R$. A function $T:V\to W$ is linear if for all $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in V$ and $c\in\R$
T(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})=T\mathbf{u}+T\mathbf{v},\qquad T(c\mathbf{v})=cT\mathbf{v}.
Equivalently $T(a\mathbf{u}+b\mathbf{v})=aT\mathbf{u}+bT\mathbf{v}$: $T$ respects linear combinations. A linear map $V\to V$ is a linear operator; a linear map $V\to\R$ is a linear functional.
If $T$ is linear then $T\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{0}$, and $T(\sum c_i\mathbf{v}_i)=\sum c_iT\mathbf{v}_i$ for every finite combination.
$T\mathbf{0}=T(0\cdot\mathbf{0})=0\cdot T\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{0}$. The second claim follows by induction from the definition.
$T_A:\R^n\to\R^m$, $T_A\mathbf{x}=A\mathbf{x}$ for any matrix $A$ (Chapter 3).
Differentiation $D:\mathcal{P}_n\to\mathcal{P}_{n-1}$, $Dp=p'$, and integration $p\mapsto\int_0^tp(s)\,ds$.
Evaluation at a point: $f\mapsto f(a)$ is a linear functional on $C[0,1]$.
The transpose $A\mapsto A\T$ on $\R^{n\times n}$, and the trace $A\mapsto\tr A$.
Multiplication by a fixed matrix $B$: $X\mapsto BX$ on $\R^{n\times n}$.
Rotation of the plane by an angle $\theta$, and reflection across a line through the origin.

$T(x)=x+1$ on $\R$ is not linear ($T0\ne0$); $T(x)=x^2$ is not linear; $T(x,y)=(xy,y)$ is not linear. A translation is not a linear map, but it is an affine map: linear plus a constant. This is why machine-learning layers $\mathbf{x}\mapsto W\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}$ are called affine, and why homogeneous coordinates (appending a $1$) turn them into linear maps in one dimension higher.

sections.title: Every linear map is a matrix

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: A linear map is determined by a basis

blocks.x: Let $(\mathbf{b}_1,\dots,\mathbf{b}_n)$ be a basis of $V$ and $\mathbf{w}_1,\dots,\mathbf{w}_n$ arbitrary vectors in $W$. Then there is exactly one linear map $T:V\to W$ with $T\mathbf{b}_i=\mathbf{w}_i$ for all $i$.

Every $\mathbf{v}$ has unique coordinates $\mathbf{v}=\sum x_i\mathbf{b}_i$ (Theorem 7.8); define $T\mathbf{v}=\sum x_i\mathbf{w}_i$. This is linear because the coordinates of $a\mathbf{u}+b\mathbf{v}$ are $a$ times those of $\mathbf{u}$ plus $b$ times those of $\mathbf{v}$. Any linear $T'$ with the same values on the basis agrees with $T$ on all combinations, hence everywhere.
So it suffices to know what a linear map does to a basis. For maps between coordinate spaces this gives a matrix.

Let $T:V\to W$ be linear, $\mathcal{B}=(\mathbf{b}_1,\dots,\mathbf{b}_n)$ a basis of $V$ and $\mathcal{C}=(\mathbf{c}_1,\dots,\mathbf{c}_m)$ a basis of $W$. The matrix of $T$ with respect to $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ is the $m\times n$ matrix $[T]_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}$ whose $j$-th column is the coordinate vector $[T\mathbf{b}_j]_{\mathcal{C}}$.
For every $\mathbf{v}\in V$,
[T\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{C}}=[T]_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}\,[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}.

Write $\mathbf{v}=\sum x_j\mathbf{b}_j$. Then $T\mathbf{v}=\sum x_jT\mathbf{b}_j$, and taking coordinates (a linear operation) gives $[T\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{C}}=\sum x_j[T\mathbf{b}_j]_{\mathcal{C}}$, which is the combination of the columns of $[T]$ with weights $x_j$.
In particular, for $T:\R^n\to\R^m$ and the standard bases, the $j$-th column of the matrix is $T\mathbf{e}_j$.
Rotation by $\theta$ counterclockwise sends $\mathbf{e}_1\mapsto(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ and $\mathbf{e}_2\mapsto(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)$, so
R_\theta=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Reflection and projection in the plane

blocks.x: Reflection across the $x$-axis sends $\mathbf{e}_1\mapsto\mathbf{e}_1$, $\mathbf{e}_2\mapsto-\mathbf{e}_2$: $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Projection onto the line through the unit vector $\mathbf{u}$ is $\mathbf{x}\mapsto\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{u}\T\mathbf{x})$, with matrix $\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}\T$ (Chapter 12). A shear $\mathbf{x}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}1&k\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\mathbf{x}$ slides each horizontal line proportionally to its height.

blocks.caption: The unit square and its images under the identity, a shear and a rotation. The image of the square is the parallelogram spanned by the columns of the matrix; its area is $\abs{\det}$.

sections.title: Kernel, image and rank–nullity for maps

blocks.x: $\ker T=\{\mathbf{v}\in V:T\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}\}$ and $\im T=\{T\mathbf{v}:\mathbf{v}\in V\}$. These are subspaces of $V$ and $W$ respectively. The rank of $T$ is $\dim\im T$ and its nullity is $\dim\ker T$.
If $V$ is finite-dimensional, $\dim V=\dim\ker T+\dim\im T$.

Choose a basis $\mathbf{k}_1,\dots,\mathbf{k}_p$ of $\ker T$ and extend to a basis $\mathbf{k}_1,\dots,\mathbf{k}_p,\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_q$ of $V$. We claim $T\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,T\mathbf{v}_q$ is a basis of $\im T$. They span: $T$ of any vector is $T(\sum a_i\mathbf{k}_i+\sum b_j\mathbf{v}_j)=\sum b_jT\mathbf{v}_j$. They are independent: if $\sum b_jT\mathbf{v}_j=\mathbf{0}$ then $\sum b_j\mathbf{v}_j\in\ker T$, so it is a combination of the $\mathbf{k}_i$, and independence of the whole basis forces all $b_j=0$. Hence $\dim V=p+q=\dim\ker T+\dim\im T$.
$T$ is injective (one-to-one) iff $\ker T=\{\mathbf{0}\}$; surjective (onto) iff $\im T=W$. If $\dim V=\dim W<\infty$, then $T$ is injective iff it is surjective iff it is bijective.

$T\mathbf{u}=T\mathbf{v}\iff T(\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{0}$, which gives the injectivity criterion. For equal finite dimensions, rank–nullity shows $\ker T=\{\mathbf{0}\}$ iff $\dim\im T=\dim V=\dim W$ iff $\im T=W$.

A bijective linear map is an isomorphism; its inverse is automatically linear. Two spaces are isomorphic iff they have the same dimension: choose bases and send one to the other (Theorem 9.5). Thus $\mathcal{P}_2$, $\R^3$ and the space of $3\times1$ matrices are all “the same” vector space.

Differentiation $D:\mathcal{P}_3\to\mathcal{P}_3$ has $\ker D=$ constants (dimension $1$) and image $\mathcal{P}_2$ (dimension $3$), consistent with $4=1+3$. It is neither injective nor surjective, even though domain and codomain have the same dimension. With respect to the basis $(1,t,t^2,t^3)$, its matrix is
whose $j$-th column holds the coordinates of $(t^{j-1})'=(j-1)t^{j-2}$.
If $S:U\to V$ and $T:V\to W$ are linear with bases $\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}$ of $U,V,W$, then $T\circ S$ is linear and
[T\circ S]_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{A}}=[T]_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}\,[S]_{\mathcal{B}\leftarrow\mathcal{A}}.

By Theorem 9.7, $[T(S\mathbf{u})]_{\mathcal{C}}=[T]_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}[S\mathbf{u}]_{\mathcal{B}}=[T]_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}[S]_{\mathcal{B}\leftarrow\mathcal{A}}[\mathbf{u}]_{\mathcal{A}}$. The unique matrix that maps $[\mathbf{u}]_{\mathcal{A}}$ to $[T\circ S\,\mathbf{u}]_{\mathcal{C}}$ for all $\mathbf{u}$ is the product.

This is the reason matrix multiplication looks strange: it is defined so that the matrix of “do $S$, then do $T$” is the product of matrices. Associativity of matrix multiplication is then obvious, since composition of functions is associative; non-commutativity is also obvious, since rotating then reflecting differs from reflecting then rotating.

Rotate by $90^\circ$ and then reflect across the $x$-axis: $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$, while the opposite order gives $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. One is a reflection across the line $y=-x$, the other across $y=x$.
A linear map is invertible (bijective) iff its matrix with respect to any bases is invertible, and $[T^{-1}]_{\mathcal{B}\leftarrow\mathcal{C}}=\big([T]_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}\big)^{-1}$.
Apply Theorem 9.14 to $T^{-1}\circ T=\id_V$ and $T\circ T^{-1}=\id_W$, and use that the matrix of the identity map with respect to one basis on both sides is $I$.

$\mathcal{P}_2$ and $\R^3$ are isomorphic, but the isomorphism depends on a choice of basis; there is no canonical identification. This is why abstract vector spaces are not merely “$\R^n$ in disguise”: properties that depend on a basis (such as “the third coordinate”) are meaningless on $\mathcal{P}_2$ until a basis is chosen. Chapter 10 studies how the matrix of one map changes when the basis does.

sections.title: Dual space and the transpose as a map

blocks.x: A linear functional $f:V\to\R$ is represented, relative to a basis, by a row vector. The set $V^*$ of all linear functionals is itself a vector space of dimension $\dim V$, the dual space. Given $T:V\to W$ the transpose map $T^*:W^*\to V^*$ sends $g$ to $g\circ T$; its matrix is the transpose $[T]\T$ with respect to dual bases. This is why $A$ and $A\T$ appear together, and it explains Theorem 8.9: $\Null A\T$ consists of the functionals that vanish on $\Col A$.

blocks.name: Interview check
blocks.title: rank of a composition and counting arguments

blocks.x: Questions such as “if $T:\R^5\to\R^3$ is onto, what is $\dim\ker T$?” are one-line applications of rank–nullity: $\dim\ker T=5-3=2$. Likewise “can a linear map from $\R^3$ onto $\R^4$ exist?” is no, because $\dim\im T\le3$. Always check these dimension counts first.
A linear map respects addition and scaling; a map is fixed by its values on a basis.
With bases chosen, a map $V\to W$ becomes a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the images of basis vectors, and $[T\mathbf{v}]=[T][\mathbf{v}]$.
$\dim V=\dim\ker T+\dim\im T$.
Composition corresponds to matrix multiplication, and inverse maps to inverse matrices.
Spaces of the same dimension are isomorphic, but not canonically.
Decide which are linear: (a) $T(x,y)=(x+y,2x)$; (b) $T(x,y)=(x,y+1)$; (c) $T(p)=p(2)$ on $\mathcal{P}_3$; (d) $T(A)=\det A$ on $\R^{2\times2}$; (e) $T(A)=A+A\T$.
Find the matrix of the linear map $T:\R^3\to\R^2$ with $T\mathbf{e}_1=(1,2)$, $T\mathbf{e}_2=(0,1)$, $T\mathbf{e}_3=(3,-1)$, and compute $T(2,1,-1)$.
Find the matrix of $D:\mathcal{P}_2\to\mathcal{P}_1$ and of $S:\mathcal{P}_1\to\mathcal{P}_2$, $Sp(t)=\int_0^tp$, in the monomial bases; compute $[D][S]$ and $[S][D]$ and interpret the results.
Show that rotation by $\alpha$ followed by rotation by $\beta$ is rotation by $\alpha+\beta$, and deduce the angle addition formulas from $R_\alpha R_\beta=R_{\alpha+\beta}$.
Let $T:\R^4\to\R^3$ have matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0&1\\0&1&1&1\\1&3&1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Find bases of $\ker T$ and $\im T$ and verify rank–nullity.
Prove that a linear map $T:V\to W$ with $\dim V>\dim W$ cannot be injective, and one with $\dim V<\dim W$ cannot be surjective.
Prove that if $T:V\to V$ satisfies $T^2=T$ (a projection) then $V=\ker T\oplus\im T$. (Hint: $\mathbf{v}=(\mathbf{v}-T\mathbf{v})+T\mathbf{v}$.)
The shift operator $S(x_1,x_2,\dots)=(0,x_1,x_2,\dots)$ on $\R^\infty$ is injective but not surjective. Does this contradict Theorem 9.12?
